segments.title: Lodging and local audiences' feeling for jazz in Asia
segments.summary: Addie describes hotels and stays with American families; Jack says Asian audiences are fascinated and already hear jazz on American radio.

segments.title: The King of Siam's own band
segments.summary: Talk about who plays with the king, his band of doctors and ministers, and his cabinet.

segments.title: Ray Bauduc's first break: barnstorming, Freddie Rich and Ben Pollack
segments.summary: Jack recounts meeting Bauduc after a cross-country barnstorm trip, then getting him a job with Ben Pollack, where he stayed years.

segments.title: Tour dates, a Cambodian flute, and hopes of a Russia tour
segments.summary: Scheduling talk of future State Department tours, a Cambodian flute and Raymond Burke, then the Asian tour dates (Sept 23 to Jan 23) and a hoped-for Russia trip.

segments.title: Why people everywhere like real jazz
segments.summary: Jack says foreign audiences love unadulterated New Orleans jazz, while modern jazz does not come naturally to them.

segments.title: The King of Thailand's love of jazz and recording
segments.summary: Jack describes the king's record collection, radio station and theater, and his taping of the whole concert.

segments.title: Jazz as freedom and the effect of tours on international relations
segments.summary: Jack quotes the King of Cambodia on freedom, tells of a university dean staying all night, and says the tours opened doors for public relations.

segments.title: Dixieland bands in Japan and how they learned
segments.summary: Addie reports an upsurge of Japanese dixieland bands; Jack says they copy records and have dropped their traditional music.

segments.title: Indian classical music, improvisation and the suppressed tradition
segments.summary: Jack describes Indian classical music and its drone; the interviewer notes improvisation was lost to classical music in the 19th century.

segments.title: Brubeck, Marian Anderson and jazz drawing crowds at the Brussels fair
segments.summary: Jack says jazz made the biggest impact compared with other US acts and drew crowds at Brussels, though the government did not supply it.

segments.title: Lasting aftereffects: music and arranging books sent to the Philippines and Burma
segments.summary: Addie and Jack describe letters, music sent to the Philippines and arranging books sent to Burma.

segments.title: Other State Department jazz tours and the length of this one
segments.summary: Jack lists tours by Dizzy and Brubeck and says theirs was longest, 120 concerts over 18 weeks, starting in Afghanistan.

segments.title: Women's school in Afghanistan and school supplies sent with Rod Alexander
segments.summary: Addie visits a girls' school in Kabul and arranges supplies to be carried by Rod Alexander's dance troupe.

segments.title: ANTA's role between Congress and the State Department
segments.summary: Explanation of ANTA as the chartered agency choosing talent on a small cultural exchange budget.

segments.title: Jack's plea for Americans to take jazz seriously at home
segments.summary: Jack says foreign admiration is somewhat erroneous, and urges Americans to value jazz over rock and roll before the old timers are gone.

segments.title: Saigon journalist's thanks to Eisenhower and goodbyes
segments.summary: Jack relays a Saigon writer's message that sending the tour was the best thing sent, then the interview ends.
